title: Tria capita ex opere quodam majori inedito de theoria lunae

deep.reconstruction:
Problem: correct the tabular node longitude and the inclination rho of the lunar orbit using the timings of a lunar eclipse. The eclipse is a total one, computed on p.378; the timings are beginning, end, immersion and emersion.

Set-up (from p.378):
- Shadow radius alpha and Moon radius beta give f = alpha+beta (contact at beginning and end) and F = alpha-beta (immersion and emersion).
- h and H are the durations between beginning and end, and between immersion and emersion.
- m, n, k are the hourly motions of Sun, Moon and node.
- a = h(n+k)/2 and b = h(m+k)/2 are the arcs moved, relative to the node, by Moon and shadow in a half-duration. A and B are the same for H.
- x is the shadow's distance from the node at mid-eclipse.
- The Moon and the shadow centre lie on two great circles through the node, inclined at rho. Points at arc p (orbit) and q (ecliptic) are separated by D with cos D = cos^2(rho/2) cos(p-q) + sin^2(rho/2) cos(p+q).
- The small angle c = (m+n+2k) sin2x tan^2(rho/2) / (sin1'' (n-m)) arcsec accounts for mid-eclipse not coinciding with the Moon-shadow configuration used. Here lg = 4.6855749 is log sin1'' with characteristic -10. I verify c = 74.7'', which is about 75''.

The contact conditions are then:
- cos f = cos^2(rho/2) cos(a-b±c) + sin^2(rho/2) cos(2x ∓ (a+b) ∓ c) at beginning and end;
- likewise with F, A, B at immersion and emersion.

Tabular start: x = shadow longitude minus true node = 9s6°51'7'' - 3s2°34'24'' = 6s4°16'43'', i.e. 4°16'43'' from the descending node.

§5:
- Eliminating sin^2(rho/2) between the f and F conditions gives d = cos(2x-a-b-c)/cos(2x-A-B-c). Hence tan2x = [d cos(A+B+c) - cos(a+b+c)] / [sin(a+b+c) - d sin(A+B+c)]. Euler gets x = 8°22'45''.
- Using rho directly, cos(2x-a-b-c) = [cos f - cos^2(rho/2) cos(a-b+c)] / sin^2(rho/2) gives x = 3°19'59''.
- Euler concludes that these formulas make the node position 'lubricum' (ill-conditioned). Both are quotients of differences of cosines near 1.

§6:
- Dividing the beginning condition by the end condition gives cos(2x-c-(a+b)) / cos(2x-c+(a+b)) = [cos f - cos^2 cos(a-b+c)] / [cos f - cos^2 cos(a-b-c)]. This is written as a tangent formula and depends only on the asymmetry 2c.
- Euler gets x = 4°10'56'', so the mean node should be advanced 5'47''.
- Inclination: sin^2(rho/2) = [cos(a-b+c) - cos f] / [2 sin(x-a-c) sin(x-b)], with the numerator rewritten as a product of sines (both identities are correct). Euler judges the angles too small for a reliable rho.

§7: The §6 method does not use immersion and emersion, so partial eclipses can be used. They are better for rho because x-a-c and x-b are larger. He takes the partial eclipse of 1731 June 19:
- the mid-time 13h57'31'' (apparent) is the exact mean of 13h14'21'' and 14h40'41'';
- 13h58'15'' is the corresponding mean time (equation of time 44s);
- the duration is 1h26'20'' = 1.4389 h, as used on p.380.

So the page is a practical least-sensitivity selection among eliminations of a nonlinear contact-condition system: an early, informal awareness of ill-conditioning in reducing observations.
errors: Small arithmetic checks (a, b, A, B, a±b, A±B, f, F, c, and the trig identities) all verify.

Recomputing d with the printed inputs I get d ≈ 1.00336 (log ≈ 0.00146), not log d = 0.001647. With d = 1.00336 the tan2x formula gives x ≈ 7°30' rather than 8°22'45''. Either way this confirms Euler's point about ill-conditioning; his own d does reproduce his x.

Recomputing the §6 equation with the printed inputs (R - 1 = 2cos^2(rho/2) sin(a-b) sin c / [cos f - cos^2(rho/2) cos(a-b-c)] ≈ 0.00585) I obtain 2x ≈ 8°34.8' and x ≈ 4°17.4'. This almost coincides with the tabular 4°16'43'', against Euler's 4°10'56''. If my reading is right, the advertised node correction of 5'47'' is a computational artifact rather than an observational result (hedged: depends on exact form of the earlier formula and on the 7-figure log practice).

Euler's verbal claim that the §6 angles are 'nimis parvi' is mild: x-a-c is about 3°7' and x-b about 4°7'. The real weakness is the small numerator cos(a-b+c) - cos f, a difference of nearly equal small arcs.

ideas.what: Determining node longitude and orbital inclination from contact timings of lunar eclipses via spherical-trigonometric contact equations
ideas.modern_name: reduction of eclipse observations for lunar orbital elements
ideas.usually_credited_to: standard 18th-century practice (Halley, Euler, Tobias Mayer, Lalande)
ideas.where_published: this text itself (Opera postuma 1862; E838); related eclipse computations in Euler's lunar works (unsure of exact locations)

ideas.what: Comparing several eliminations of the same nonlinear system and rejecting those whose results are unstable ('lubricum')
ideas.modern_name: ill-conditioning / sensitivity analysis in reduction of observations
ideas.usually_credited_to: implicit in Mayer (1750) and Laplace; formal theory by Gauss/Legendre (least squares) and later condition-number notions
ideas.where_published: Euler's 1749 Saturn prize memoir (E120) shows his handling of inconsistent equations; this specific remark only here

ideas.what: Formula using only first and last contacts (the asymmetry angle c), making partial eclipses usable for node and inclination
ideas.modern_name: using eclipse contact asymmetry to fix node distance
ideas.where_published: E838 only, as far as I know

ideas.what: Small correction angle c ∝ (m+n+2k) sin2x tan^2(rho/2)/(n-m)
ideas.modern_name: reduction of mid-eclipse to opposition in orbit/ecliptic

missed.claim: Recomputation suggests the §6 node determination should give x ≈ 4°17', essentially the tabular value, not 4°10'56''. The 5'47'' 'correction' of the mean node is probably an arithmetic artifact; log d is also off (0.00146 vs 0.001647).
missed.quote: reperitur 2x = 8°21'52'' et x = 4°10'56'' ... locus nodi medius hac particula 5'47'' promovendus videatur
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: Relevant to historians assessing the accuracy of Euler's lunar tables and his empirical node corrections. A minor erratum for the Opera omnia commentary.

missed.claim: An explicit, numerically demonstrated recognition of ill-conditioning: algebraically equivalent eliminations give x = 8°23', 3°20' and 4°11'. Euler chooses the formula least sensitive to the data and argues that partial eclipses give better-conditioned denominators.
missed.quote: unde patet ex his formulis nimis esse lubricum locum nodi assignare
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: A small but citable example in the prehistory of numerical conditioning and the design of observations. It is probably not singled out in the histories of error theory.

deep.surprise_reason: Routine applied eclipse reduction. The only notable features are the explicit numerical demonstration of ill-conditioning with the resulting choice of a better-conditioned formula, and a probable arithmetic error that makes the claimed node correction spurious.
transcription_corrections: The c formula's 'sec.' means the result is in arcseconds. lg = 4,6855749 is log sin 1'' (characteristic -10), not log of a large number.
The transcription matches the image otherwise; 'ld = 0,001647' and 'x = 3°19'59''' read correctly from the scan.
